endorsements.quote: Layer 1 assigns each vibe-coding activity to one of four risk tiers using four criteria: data sensitivity (is PHI involved?), clinical-decision proximity (does the output inform a treatment decision?), user autonomy (can the clinician independently verify the output?), and scale of impact (does the artefact affect an individual or an institution?).

First, an intake and triage form on which a clinician scores a proposed tool against the four Layer-1 criteria and routes it to a clinical-informatics or AI-governance committee; the form yields a tier and a role in minutes.
Third, an accountability register recording, for each deployed tool, its tier, clinical purpose, owner, and review date—the minimum needed to satisfy an audit.

In parallel, three actions are available now: health systems should adopt tiered acceptable-use policies that name a tier, a role, and an owner; regulators should clarify how generative, non-deterministic clinical tools enter existing frameworks before the EU AI Act’s August 2027 deadline; and professional bodies should incorporate agentic-coding competencies into clinical-informatics training, building on recent competency work ( Cao et al., 2026 ).
Layer 3 binds the regulatory obligations and the named accountability owner appropriate to that tier and role.
Layer 2 sets the quality bar that the resulting artefact must meet, with thresholds that rise with the tier.
Layer 3 maps regulation onto the tiers, clarifying which obligations apply and at what point they become mandatory ( Table 5 ).

Code Provenance Transparency (CPT) is the documented record of prompts, model versions, intermediate outputs, and human edits—the audit trail without which post-hoc safety review is impossible, and a direct answer to the call for code-provenance documentation ( Moore and Tatonetti, 2025a ).

Hallucination Resilience (HR) is the demonstrated capacity of the artefact to fail safely when the model has fabricated APIs, packages, or logic, tested through adversarial prompting, dependency verification against trusted registries, and runtime checks on critical paths.

unlisted_practices: Require named clinician-developer role archetypes for AI-generated software, with clinical vibe coding restricted to a requirements-analyst role and engineering teams writing and validating code for highest-risk clinical tools.
Require clinician-developers to be able to explain the AI-generated code they deploy, measured as comprehension coverage at code review, with the required threshold rising by risk tier.
Scan dependencies of AI-generated software against trusted package registries and perform security scanning to catch hallucinated or non-existent packages.
Require engineering co-development and formal testing for PHI-touching or clinical-workflow tools built through AI code generation.

screen.reason: This paper presents the VIBE-HI conceptual governance framework to guide the evaluation, appropriateness, quality, and safety of clinical vibe coding (LLM-based natural language software generation in health care).
